claim: PRDM9 specifies hotspots of meiotic recombination.
source: PR domain containing 9 (Prdm9) is specifying hotspots of meiotic recombination but in hybrids between two mouse subspecies Prdm9 controls failure of meiotic chromosome synapsis and hybrid male sterility.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript (Baudat et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010).

claim: In hybrids between two mouse subspecies, Prdm9 controls failure of meiotic chromosome synapsis and hybrid male sterility.
source: PR domain containing 9 (Prdm9) is specifying hotspots of meiotic recombination but in hybrids between two mouse subspecies Prdm9 controls failure of meiotic chromosome synapsis and hybrid male sterility.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous research cited in the manuscript (Mihola et al., 2009; Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012; Forejt et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).

claim: Prdm9-controlled asynapsis and meiotic arrest are conditioned by the inter-subspecific heterozygosity of the hybrid genome.
source: We have previously reported that Prdm9-controlled asynapsis and meiotic arrest are conditioned by the inter-subspecific heterozygosity of the hybrid genome and we presumed that the insufficient number of properly repaired PRDM9-dependent DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) causes asynapsis of chromosomes and meiotic arrest (Gregorova et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on previous work by the authors (Gregorova et al., 2018).

claim: The insufficient number of properly repaired PRDM9-dependent DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) causes asynapsis of chromosomes and meiotic arrest.
source: We have previously reported that Prdm9-controlled asynapsis and meiotic arrest are conditioned by the inter-subspecific heterozygosity of the hybrid genome and we presumed that the insufficient number of properly repaired PRDM9-dependent DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) causes asynapsis of chromosomes and meiotic arrest (Gregorova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their previous work.

claim: A single injection of cisplatin increased frequency of RPA and DMC1 foci at the zygotene stage of sterile hybrids.
source: A single injection of chemotherapeutic drug cisplatin increased frequency of RPA and DMC1 foci at the zygotene stage of sterile hybrids, enhanced homolog recognition and increased the proportion of spermatocytes with fully synapsed homologs at pachytene.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Cisplatin enhanced homolog recognition in sterile hybrids.
source: A single injection of chemotherapeutic drug cisplatin increased frequency of RPA and DMC1 foci at the zygotene stage of sterile hybrids, enhanced homolog recognition and increased the proportion of spermatocytes with fully synapsed homologs at pachytene.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased synapsis observed in the experiments.

claim: Cisplatin increased the proportion of spermatocytes with fully synapsed homologs at pachytene.
source: A single injection of chemotherapeutic drug cisplatin increased frequency of RPA and DMC1 foci at the zygotene stage of sterile hybrids, enhanced homolog recognition and increased the proportion of spermatocytes with fully synapsed homologs at pachytene.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The results bring new evidence for a DSB-dependent mechanism of synapsis failure and infertility of intersubspecific hybrids.
source: The results bring a new evidence for a DSB-dependent mechanism of synapsis failure and infertility of intersubspecific hybrids.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Proper synapsis of homologous chromosomes is an important meiotic checkpoint preventing germline transfer of harmful genic and chromosomal mutations to the next generations.
source: Proper synapsis of homologous chromosomes is an important meiotic checkpoint preventing germline transfer of harmful genic and chromosomal mutations to the next generations (Schimenti, 2005; Zickler and Kleckner, 2015; Rinaldi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Synapsis of homologous chromosomes is initiated at the leptotene stage of the first meiotic prophase by induction of developmentally programmed, SPO11-induced DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: Synapsis of homologous chromosomes is initiated at the leptotene stage of the first meiotic prophase by induction of developmentally programmed, SPO11-induced DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) (Keeney et al., 1997; Keeney et al., 1999; Romanienko and Camerini-Otero, 2000).
evidence: This is well-established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: After 5' to 3' resection of each end of DSB, replication protein A (RPA) binds the 3' overhang to save it from degradation.
source: After 5' to 3' resection of each end of DSB, replication protein A (RPA) binds the 3' overhang to save it from degradation, later being displaced by RAD51 and DMC1 recombinases (Inagaki et al., 2010) but see (Moens et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DSB repair mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: RPA is later displaced by RAD51 and DMC1 recombinases.
source: After 5' to 3' resection of each end of DSB, replication protein A (RPA) binds the 3' overhang to save it from degradation, later being displaced by RAD51 and DMC1 recombinases (Inagaki et al., 2010) but see (Moens et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge with some controversy noted by the 'but see' citation.

claim: The resulting nucleoprotein filament is engaged in homology search in the process leading to DSBs repair by homologous recombination and to synapsis of homologous chromosomes.
source: The resulting nucleoprotein filament is engaged in homology search in the process leading to DSBs repair by homologous recombination and to synapsis of homologous chromosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of homologous recombination.

claim: SPO11-induced DSBs are nonrandomly clustered into narrow 1–2 kilobase-pair intervals called recombination hotspots.
source: The SPO11-induced DSBs are nonrandomly clustered into narrow 1–2 kilobase-pair intervals called recombination hotspots and their localization is predetermined by the PRDM9 binding to specific motifs inside these intervals and PRDM9-driven induced trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 and lysine 36 on adjacent nucleosomes (Baudat et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Eram et al., 2014; Lange et al., 2016; Powers et al., 2016, for recent reviews see Grey et al., 2018 and Paigen and Petkov, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The localization of recombination hotspots is predetermined by PRDM9 binding to specific motifs inside these intervals.
source: The SPO11-induced DSBs are nonrandomly clustered into narrow 1–2 kilobase-pair intervals called recombination hotspots and their localization is predetermined by the PRDM9 binding to specific motifs inside these intervals and PRDM9-driven induced trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 and lysine 36 on adjacent nucleosomes (Baudat et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Eram et al., 2014; Lange et al., 2016; Powers et al., 2016, for recent reviews see Grey et al., 2018 and Paigen and Petkov, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: PRDM9 binding induces trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 and lysine 36 on adjacent nucleosomes.
source: The SPO11-induced DSBs are nonrandomly clustered into narrow 1–2 kilobase-pair intervals called recombination hotspots and their localization is predetermined by the PRDM9 binding to specific motifs inside these intervals and PRDM9-driven induced trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 and lysine 36 on adjacent nucleosomes (Baudat et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Eram et al., 2014; Lange et al., 2016; Powers et al., 2016, for recent reviews see Grey et al., 2018 and Paigen and Petkov, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Prdm9 acts as the major hybrid sterility gene in certain hybrids between house mouse subspecies of Mus m. musculus (mouse strain PWD) and Mus m. domesticus (mouse strain C57BL/6).
source: The Prdm9 gene, besides determining position of the recombination hotspots, acts as the major hybrid sterility gene in certain hybrids between house mouse subspecies of Mus m. musculus (mouse strain PWD) and Mus m. domesticus (mouse strain C57BL/6, hereafter B6) (Mihola et al., 2009; Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012; Forejt et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations from previous research.

claim: Disrupted synapsis of homologous chromosomes and dysregulation of meiotic sex chromosome inactivation are two major cellular phenotypes controlled by the Prdm9 gene in sterile (PWD x B6)F1 hybrids.
source: Disrupted synapsis of homologous chromosomes and dysregulation of meiotic sex chromosome inactivation are two major cellular phenotypes controlled by the Prdm9 gene in sterile (PWD x B6)F1 (hereafter PBF1) hybrids (Forejt and Iványi, 1974; Mihola et al., 2009; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014; Gregorova et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations from previous research.

claim: When the mouse Prdm9 gene was 'humanized' by substitution of the C2H2 zinc-finger (ZnF) DNA-binding domain for its human ortholog, the humanized PBF1-Prdm9Hu/PWD meiocytes regained normal meiotic pairing and hybrid males became fertile.
source: When the mouse Prdm9 gene was 'humanized' by substitution of the C2H2 zinc-finger (ZnF) DNA-binding domain for its human ortholog, the humanized PBF1-Prdm9Hu/PWD meiocytes regained normal meiotic pairing and hybrid males became fertile.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Davies et al., 2016.

claim: The humanization of Prdm9 provided direct evidence for the role of PRDM9 ZnF array in the control of hybrid sterility.
source: This unexpected finding provided direct evidence for the role of PRDM9 ZnF array in the control of hybrid sterility (Davies et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results from Davies et al., 2016.

claim: The asynapsis and male sterility are proposed to be mainly a consequence of the evolutionary erosion of PRDM9 binding sites.
source: The asynapsis and male sterility were proposed to be mainly a consequence of the evolutionary erosion of PRDM9 binding sites (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on previous work, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Heterozygous allelic sites with lower PRDM9 binding affinity are used preferentially as a template for DSB repair in gene-conversion events.
source: Because the heterozygous allelic sites with lower PRDM9 binding affinity are used preferentially as a template for DSB repair in gene-conversion events, the sites with higher binding affinity mutate much faster than the rest of the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of hotspot erosion.

claim: Sites with higher PRDM9 binding affinity mutate much faster than the rest of the genome.
source: Because the heterozygous allelic sites with lower PRDM9 binding affinity are used preferentially as a template for DSB repair in gene-conversion events, the sites with higher binding affinity mutate much faster than the rest of the genome.
evidence: This is a consequence of biased gene conversion at recombination hotspots.

claim: The majority of the PRDM9PWD-determined hotspots in PBF1 sterile males are found on B6 homologs and vice versa.
source: As a result, the majority of the PRDM9PWD-determined hotspots in PBF1 sterile males are found on B6 homologs and vice versa.
evidence: This is based on the erosion hypothesis and supported by data from Davies et al., 2016.

claim: Hotspot asymmetry can result in a delay or inability to repair DSBs using homologous chromosome as a template, thus preventing successful pairing and synapsis of homologs.
source: Such hotspot asymmetry can result in a delay or inability to repair DSBs using homologous chromosome as a template, thus preventing successful pairing and synapsis of homologs (Davies et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed by Davies et al., 2016.

claim: Eroded PRDM9B6 binding sites are not recognized or hardly recognized by the PRDM9B6 zinc-finger array in B6 meiosis.
source: Eroded PRDM9B6 binding sites are not recognized or hardly recognized by the PRDM9B6 zinc-finger array in B6 meiosis, but the same sites were saved from erosion during the evolution of the other subspecies.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and is part of the erosion hypothesis.

claim: In (PWD x B6)F1 hybrids PRDM9B6 often binds to the sites on PWD chromosome that are erased on B6 homolog.
source: Thus, in (PWD x B6)F1 hybrids PRDM9B6 often binds to the sites on PWD chromosome that are erased on B6 homolog and, vice versa, PRDM9PWD more often binds to the sites on B6 homolog, eroded in PWD.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and is part of the asymmetry hypothesis.

claim: PRDM9PWD more often binds to the sites on B6 homolog, eroded in PWD.
source: Thus, in (PWD x B6)F1 hybrids PRDM9B6 often binds to the sites on PWD chromosome that are erased on B6 homolog and, vice versa, PRDM9PWD more often binds to the sites on B6 homolog, eroded in PWD.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and is part of the asymmetry hypothesis.

claim: The proportion of asymmetric sites exceeds 70% of all DSBs in (PWD x B6)F1 hybrid meiosis.
source: The proportion of such asymmetric sites exceeds 70% of all DSBs in (PWD x B6)F1 hybrid meiosis (Davies et al., 2016) and interferes with chromosome synapsis and meiotic progression.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from Davies et al., 2016.

claim: Asymmetric hotspots interfere with chromosome synapsis and meiotic progression.
source: The proportion of such asymmetric sites exceeds 70% of all DSBs in (PWD x B6)F1 hybrid meiosis (Davies et al., 2016) and interferes with chromosome synapsis and meiotic progression.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between asymmetric hotspots and synapsis failure.

claim: The higher activity of asymmetric hotspots estimated by DMC1-ChIP-seq is explained by a delay or failure of DSB repair.
source: The higher activity of these asymmetric hotspots estimated by DMC1-ChIP-seq is explained by a delay or failure of DSB repair.
evidence: This is an interpretation of ChIP-seq data from Davies et al., 2016.

claim: When synapsis of the four chromosomes most strongly affected by asynapsis in the sterile hybrids was restored, male fertility was regained.
source: When synapsis of the four chromosomes most strongly affected by asynapsis in the sterile hybrids was restored in this way, male fertility was regained (Gregorova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Cisplatin is known to create DNA inter-strand (ICL) and intra-strand cross-links.
source: Cisplatin (cis-platinum diamminedichloride, hereafter cisPt) is known to create DNA inter-strand (ICL) and intra-strand cross-links.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cisplatin's mechanism of action.

claim: In replicating yeast and mammalian somatic cells removal of ICLs results in DNA DSBs.
source: In replicating yeast and mammalian somatic cells removal of ICLs results in DNA DSBs, which can be repaired by the nonhomologous end joining or by homologous recombination, the latter being favored in the germline (Lawrence et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ICL-induced DSBs can be repaired by nonhomologous end joining or by homologous recombination, the latter being favored in the germline.
source: In replicating yeast and mammalian somatic cells removal of ICLs results in DNA DSBs, which can be repaired by the nonhomologous end joining or by homologous recombination, the latter being favored in the germline (Lawrence et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Removal of cisPt-DNA adducts without creating DSBs was reported in quiescent somatic cells.
source: Removal of the cisPt-DNA adducts without creating DSBs was reported in quiescent somatic cells (Frankenberg-Schwager et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study.

claim: In the mouse, cisPt was reported to increase meiotic crossing-over.
source: In the mouse, cisPt was reported to increase meiotic crossing-over (Hanneman et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study.

claim: Significant improvement of meiotic chromosome synapsis was observed in SPO11-/- meiocytes treated with cisPt or X rays.
source: Moreover, significant improvement of meiotic chromosome synapsis was observed in SPO11-/- meiocytes treated with cisPt or X rays, indicating that exogenous DSBs can at least partially substitute the role of the SPO11-induced DSBs in pairing of homologous chromosomes (Romanienko and Camerini-Otero, 2000; Carofiglio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies.

claim: Exogenous DSBs can at least partially substitute the role of the SPO11-induced DSBs in pairing of homologous chromosomes.
source: Moreover, significant improvement of meiotic chromosome synapsis was observed in SPO11-/- meiocytes treated with cisPt or X rays, indicating that exogenous DSBs can at least partially substitute the role of the SPO11-induced DSBs in pairing of homologous chromosomes (Romanienko and Camerini-Otero, 2000; Carofiglio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that exogenous DSBs improve synapsis in SPO11-/- cells.

claim: The duration of the meiotic S-phase is 20 hr.
source: Based on the published estimates of duration of the meiotic S-phase (20 hr), leptotene (24–48 hr), zygotene (24–32 hr) and pachytene (160 hr) stages of the first meiotic prophase (OAKBERG, 1956; Oud et al., 1979; Goetz et al., 1984) the males were sacrificed 40 hr after cisPt and EdU injection to quantify the DSBs at the first meiotic prophase, or after 8 days to monitor the chromosome synapsis at the pachytene stage.
evidence: This is based on published estimates from previous studies.

claim: The duration of leptotene is 24–48 hr.
source: Based on the published estimates of duration of the meiotic S-phase (20 hr), leptotene (24–48 hr), zygotene (24–32 hr) and pachytene (160 hr) stages of the first meiotic prophase (OAKBERG, 1956; Oud et al., 1979; Goetz et al., 1984) the males were sacrificed 40 hr after cisPt and EdU injection to quantify the DSBs at the first meiotic prophase, or after 8 days to monitor the chromosome synapsis at the pachytene stage.
evidence: This is based on published estimates from previous studies.

claim: The duration of zygotene is 24–32 hr.
source: Based on the published estimates of duration of the meiotic S-phase (20 hr), leptotene (24–48 hr), zygotene (24–32 hr) and pachytene (160 hr) stages of the first meiotic prophase (OAKBERG, 1956; Oud et al., 1979; Goetz et al., 1984) the males were sacrificed 40 hr after cisPt and EdU injection to quantify the DSBs at the first meiotic prophase, or after 8 days to monitor the chromosome synapsis at the pachytene stage.
evidence: This is based on published estimates from previous studies.

claim: The duration of pachytene is 160 hr.
source: Based on the published estimates of duration of the meiotic S-phase (20 hr), leptotene (24–48 hr), zygotene (24–32 hr) and pachytene (160 hr) stages of the first meiotic prophase (OAKBERG, 1956; Oud et al., 1979; Goetz et al., 1984) the males were sacrificed 40 hr after cisPt and EdU injection to quantify the DSBs at the first meiotic prophase, or after 8 days to monitor the chromosome synapsis at the pachytene stage.
evidence: This is based on published estimates from previous studies.

claim: 40 hr after EdU and CisPt injection, 84.1 ± 3.3% of leptonemas were EdU-positive.
source: Forty hours after cisPt and EdU injection, 84.1 ± 3.3% (mean ±SE) of leptonemas and 49.3 ± 2.2% of zygonemas were EdU-positive, thus being at the S-phase at the time of injection or shortly after that.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 40 hr after EdU and CisPt injection, 49.3 ± 2.2% of zygonemas were EdU-positive.
source: Forty hours after cisPt and EdU injection, 84.1 ± 3.3% (mean ±SE) of leptonemas and 49.3 ± 2.2% of zygonemas were EdU-positive, thus being at the S-phase at the time of injection or shortly after that.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EdU-negative leptonemas (15.9%) most likely started their S-phase 20 hr or more after EdU injection, after assumed depletion of free EdU.
source: The EdU-negative leptonemas (15.9%) most likely started their S-phase 20 hr or more after EdU injection, after assumed depletion of free EdU (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1), while EdU-negative zygonemas finished their DNA replication before CisPt and EdU injection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of EdU incorporation and cell cycle progression.

claim: EdU-negative zygonemas finished their DNA replication before CisPt and EdU injection.
source: The EdU-negative leptonemas (15.9%) most likely started their S-phase 20 hr or more after EdU injection, after assumed depletion of free EdU (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1), while EdU-negative zygonemas finished their DNA replication before CisPt and EdU injection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of EdU incorporation and cell cycle progression.

claim: All pachynemas finished DNA replication before the treatment and were EdU-negative.
source: All pachynemas finished DNA replication before the treatment and were EdU-negative (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The occurrence of EdU-positive cells fitted better with the shorter reported estimates of the duration of leptotene and zygotene stages.
source: The occurrence of EdU-positive cells fitted better with the shorter reported estimates of the duration of leptotene and zygotene stages.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the observed EdU-positive cell frequencies with published stage durations.

claim: RPA protein binds ssDNA soon after resection of DSBs in mitotic and meiotic cells.
source: Since the RPA protein was reported to bind ssDNA soon after resection of DSBs in mitotic and meiotic cells (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Pacheco et al., 2018), we used the RPA foci as an early cytological marker of DSBs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cells treated with 10 mg/kg of cisPt showed significant increase of RPA foci in leptotene and zygotene stages.
source: We found out that in spite of the large variation in the number of RPA foci in individual leptonemas and zygonemas (see also Kauppi et al., 2013), cells treated with 10 mg/kg of cisPt showed significant increase of RPA foci in leptotene and zygotene stages (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The leptotene median number of 162 RPA foci per cell in control males increased to 229 foci in males treated with 10 mg/kg of cisPt (p=0.0313 Mann-Whitney U test).
source: The leptotene median number of 162 RPA foci per cell in control males increased to 229 foci in males treated with 10 mg/kg of cisPt (p=0.0313 Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Control zygotene median of 194 RPA foci increased to 210.5 foci after treatment with 10 mg/kg of cisPt (p=0.0483).
source: Control zygotene median of 194 RPA foci increased to 210.5 foci after treatment with 10 mg/kg of cisPt (p=0.0483).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The numbers of RPA foci decline at the pachytene stage of meiotic prophase in fertile male mice.
source: The numbers of RPA foci decline at the pachytene stage of meiotic prophase in fertile male mice (Li et al., 2007; Inagaki et al., 2010) but persist in high numbers in sterile untreated hybrids (median 119 RPA foci per pachynema).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RPA foci persist in high numbers in sterile untreated hybrids (median 119 RPA foci per pachynema).
source: The numbers of RPA foci decline at the pachytene stage of meiotic prophase in fertile male mice (Li et al., 2007; Inagaki et al., 2010) but persist in high numbers in sterile untreated hybrids (median 119 RPA foci per pachynema).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: CisPt did not affect frequency of RPA foci in pachynemas 40 hr after injection.
source: CisPt did not affect frequency of RPA foci in pachynemas 40 hr after injection (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RPA foci persisted in early pachynemas of fertile controls.
source: Unexpectedly, but in accord with Moens et al. (2007), the RPA foci persisted in early pachynemas of fertile controls, but significantly dropped in mid pachynemas (median 38 and 14 RPA foci in PWD and B6 compared to 98 foci in PBF1, p<0.0001) and virtually disappeared at the late pachytene stage.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, consistent with previous findings.

claim: RPA foci significantly dropped in mid pachynemas (median 38 and 14 RPA foci in PWD and B6 compared to 98 foci in PBF1, p<0.0001).
source: Unexpectedly, but in accord with Moens et al. (2007), the RPA foci persisted in early pachynemas of fertile controls, but significantly dropped in mid pachynemas (median 38 and 14 RPA foci in PWD and B6 compared to 98 foci in PBF1, p<0.0001) and virtually disappeared at the late pachytene stage.
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: RPA foci virtually disappeared at the late pachytene stage in fertile controls.
source: Unexpectedly, but in accord with Moens et al. (2007), the RPA foci persisted in early pachynemas of fertile controls, but significantly dropped in mid pachynemas (median 38 and 14 RPA foci in PWD and B6 compared to 98 foci in PBF1, p<0.0001) and virtually disappeared at the late pachytene stage.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Only EdU-positive zygotene cells showed a significant increase in the cisPt dosage-dependent RPA foci.
source: Surprisingly, when zygonemas were split to EdU-positive and negative, only EdU-positive cells showed a significant increase in the cisPt dosage-dependent RPA foci (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The doses of 1 mg/kg, 5 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg of injected cisPt increased the median of RPA foci from 200.5 in controls to 239, 255 and 250, respectively (p=0.0043, 0.0026 and 0.0006, Mann-Whitney U test).
source: The doses of 1 mg/kg, 5 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg of injected cisPt increased the median of RPA foci from 200.5 in controls to 239, 255 and 250, respectively (p=0.0043, 0.0026 and 0.0006, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Approximately half of the zygonemas were EdU-negative, apparently finishing S-phase before EdU and CisPt injection.
source: As shown above, approximately half of the zygonemas were EdU-negative, apparently finishing S-phase before EdU and CisPt injection, while the EdU-positive zygonemas were in the mid or late S-phase at the time of the treatment.
evidence: This is an inference from the EdU labeling data.

claim: EdU-positive zygonemas were in the mid or late S-phase at the time of the treatment.
source: As shown above, approximately half of the zygonemas were EdU-negative, apparently finishing S-phase before EdU and CisPt injection, while the EdU-positive zygonemas were in the mid or late S-phase at the time of the treatment.
evidence: This is an inference from the EdU labeling data.

claim: The cisPt-induced DSBs could arise anytime during the meiotic S-phase and/or at the beginning of leptotene stage.
source: Since little is known about the timing of enzymatic removal of cisPt interstrand crosslinks (Johnsson et al., 1995), the formation of DSBs cannot be precisely specified in respect of the end of DNA replication. The cisPt-induced DSBs could arise anytime during the meiotic S-phase and/or at the beginning of leptotene stage.
evidence: This is speculation based on limited knowledge about the timing of ICL removal.

claim: RPA is an ssDNA-binding protein that could mark other forms of DNA damage beside DSBs.
source: Since RPA is an ssDNA-binding protein, it could mark other forms of DNA damage beside DSBs (Wang et al., 2005); therefore, we quantified the foci of DNA meiotic recombination 1 (DMC1), a meiosis-specific strand exchange protein, which is recruited to SPO11-induced DSBs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: DMC1 is a meiosis-specific strand exchange protein, which is recruited to SPO11-induced DSBs.
source: Since RPA is an ssDNA-binding protein, it could mark other forms of DNA damage beside DSBs (Wang et al., 2005); therefore, we quantified the foci of DNA meiotic recombination 1 (DMC1), a meiosis-specific strand exchange protein, which is recruited to SPO11-induced DSBs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DMC1 function.

claim: The DMC1 response to cisPt was similar to that of RPA.
source: The DMC1 response to cisPt was similar to that of RPA.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results for RPA and DMC1.

claim: The combined EdU-positive and -negative zygonemas showed an enhancing effect of cisPt on the frequency of DMC1 foci.
source: The combined EdU-positive and -negative zygonemas showed an enhancing effect of cisPt on the frequency of DMC1 foci (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The median number of DMC1 foci increased from 215 to 241, 233 and 251 after 1, 5 and 10 mg/kg of cisPt (p=0.0208, 0.0263 and 0.0048, Mann-Whitney U), respectively.
source: The median number of DMC1 foci increased from 215 to 241, 233 and 251 after 1, 5 and 10 mg/kg of cisPt (p=0.0208, 0.0263 and 0.0048, Mann-Whitney U), respectively.
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: CisPt treatment did not influence the high frequency of DMC1 foci in PBF1 spermatocytes at pachytene stage.
source: CisPt treatment did not influence the high frequency of DMC1 foci in PBF1 spermatocytes at pachytene stage.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: DMC1 foci significantly dropped in early pachynemas of fertile PWD and B6 controls (median 60 and 31 DMC1 foci in PWD and B6 compared to 111 foci in PBF1, p<0.0001).
source: Contrary to RPA, the DMC1 foci significantly dropped (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) in early pachynemas of fertile PWD and B6 controls (median 60 and 31 DMC1 foci in PWD and B6 compared to 111 foci in PBF1, p<0.0001) and virtually disappeared at the mid pachytene stage (median 10 and 0 of DMC1 foci in PWD and B6 compared to 85 foci in PBF1, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: DMC1 foci virtually disappeared at the mid pachytene stage in fertile controls (median 10 and 0 of DMC1 foci in PWD and B6 compared to 85 foci in PBF1, p<0.0001).
source: Contrary to RPA, the DMC1 foci significantly dropped (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) in early pachynemas of fertile PWD and B6 controls (median 60 and 31 DMC1 foci in PWD and B6 compared to 111 foci in PBF1, p<0.0001) and virtually disappeared at the mid pachytene stage (median 10 and 0 of DMC1 foci in PWD and B6 compared to 85 foci in PBF1, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: EdU-positive zygonemas showed a significant increase of DMC1 foci at all three cisPt concentrations.
source: When split according to the EdU phenotype, the EdU-positive zygonemas showed a significant increase of DMC1 foci at all three concentrations (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 2), from 225.5 to 260.5, 269 and 259.5 foci, respectively (p=0.0025, 0.0192 and 0.0442, Mann-Whitney U test), while in EdU-negative cells the steady DMC1 increase became significant at 10 mg/kg dose (p=0.0246).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In EdU-negative cells the steady DMC1 increase became significant at 10 mg/kg dose (p=0.0246).
source: When split according to the EdU phenotype, the EdU-positive zygonemas showed a significant increase of DMC1 foci at all three concentrations (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 2), from 225.5 to 260.5, 269 and 259.5 foci, respectively (p=0.0025, 0.0192 and 0.0442, Mann-Whitney U test), while in EdU-negative cells the steady DMC1 increase became significant at 10 mg/kg dose (p=0.0246).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The control males displayed the mean frequency of 8.61% (5.80; 12.12) (95% CI) of fully synapsed pachynemas.
source: The control males displayed the mean frequency of 8.61% (5.80; 12.12) (95% CI) of fully synapsed pachynemas in contrast to the males treated with 5 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg of cisPt, which showed a threefold increase of fully synapsed pachynemas, 24.68% (19.41; 30.49) (p=1.6 × 10−9, Tukey's post-hoc test) and 28.71% (22.86; 35.08) (p=7.3 × 10−13), respectively (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Males treated with 5 mg/kg cisPt showed 24.68% (19.41; 30.49) fully synapsed pachynemas (p=1.6 × 10−9, Tukey's post-hoc test).
source: The control males displayed the mean frequency of 8.61% (5.80; 12.12) (95% CI) of fully synapsed pachynemas in contrast to the males treated with 5 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg of cisPt, which showed a threefold increase of fully synapsed pachynemas, 24.68% (19.41; 30.49) (p=1.6 × 10−9, Tukey's post-hoc test) and 28.71% (22.86; 35.08) (p=7.3 × 10−13), respectively (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Males treated with 10 mg/kg cisPt showed 28.71% (22.86; 35.08) fully synapsed pachynemas (p=7.3 × 10−13).
source: The control males displayed the mean frequency of 8.61% (5.80; 12.12) (95% CI) of fully synapsed pachynemas in contrast to the males treated with 5 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg of cisPt, which showed a threefold increase of fully synapsed pachynemas, 24.68% (19.41; 30.49) (p=1.6 × 10−9, Tukey's post-hoc test) and 28.71% (22.86; 35.08) (p=7.3 × 10−13), respectively (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The percentage of pachynemas with fully synapsed bivalents dramatically increased from 5.66% in the control male (0 mg/kg of cisPt) to 48.78% and 46.70% in the males on the 7th and 8th day after treatment.
source: The percentage of pachynemas with fully synapsed bivalents dramatically increased from 5.66% in the control male (0 mg/kg of cisPt) to 48.78% and 46.70% in the males on the 7th and 8th day after treatment (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the pilot experiment.

claim: The cisPt treatment caused a nonsignificant increase of fully synapsed early pachynemas.
source: While the cisPt treatment caused a nonsignificant increase of fully synapsed early pachynemas, the enhancement of synapsis was dramatic in mid-late pachynemas (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The enhancement of synapsis was dramatic in mid-late pachynemas.
source: While the cisPt treatment caused a nonsignificant increase of fully synapsed early pachynemas, the enhancement of synapsis was dramatic in mid-late pachynemas (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The efficiency of repair of cisPt-induced DSBs by standard homologous recombination is low in general and/or a significant fraction of spermatocytes carrying them do not survive until early pachytene stage.
source: We assume that the efficiency of repair of cisPt-induced DSBs by standard homologous recombination is low in general and/or that a significant fraction of spermatocytes carrying them do not survive until early pachytene stage.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the observed pattern of synapsis improvement.

claim: Spermatocytes with multiple asynapsed autosomes that survive to the early pachytene stage are mostly eliminated before reaching the mid-late pachytene stage.
source: Those spermatocytes with multiple asynapsed autosomes that survive to the early pachytene stage are mostly eliminated before reaching the mid-late pachytene stage as reported previously (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on previous findings cited in the manuscript.

claim: The synapsis was marginally significantly more frequent (p=0.0433, GLM model) in EdU-negative than in EdU-positive pachynemas.
source: When divided according the cell cycle stage at the time of cisPt injection, the synapsis was marginally significantly more frequent (p=0.0433, GLM model) in EdU-negative than in EdU-positive pachynemas (Figure 5E), on average 1.69 times (1.02; 2.84, 95 % CI; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: EdU-negative fully synapsed pachynemas could arise from a subset of cells with exogenous DSBs generated at leptotene/early zygotene at the time of cisPt and EdU injection.
source: The EdU-negative fully synapsed pachynemas could arise from a subset of cells with exogenous DSBs generated at leptotene/early zygotene at the time of cisPt and EdU injection.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the EdU-negative synapsis improvement.

claim: EdU-positive cells that were at the preleptotene S-phase at the time of injection removed the cisPt induced ICLs at early leptotene stage.
source: It is tempting to suggest that also the EdU-positive cells that were at the preleptotene S-phase at the time of injection removed the cisPt induced ICLs at early leptotene stage.
evidence: This is speculation about the timing of ICL removal.

claim: No sperm was found in the ductus epididymis of the males 30 days after injection.
source: No sperm was found in the ductus epididymis of the males 30 days after injection.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment.

claim: Histological sections showed atrophy of seminiferous tubules caused by the lethal effect of cisPt on proliferating spermatogonia and somatic cells of seminiferous tubules.
source: Histological sections showed atrophy of seminiferous tubules caused by the lethal effect of cisPt on proliferating spermatogonia and somatic cells of seminiferous tubules (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from histological analysis.

claim: In untreated control hybrids the late pachynemas represented 2.03% (4/107) of all pachynemas recorded from the meiotic spreads.
source: While in untreated control hybrids the late pachynemas represented 2.03% (4/107) of all pachynemas recorded from the meiotic spreads, the frequency increased to 12.12% (28/231) and 13.10% (30/229) after 5 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg cisPt treatment, respectively.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The frequency of late pachynemas increased to 12.12% (28/231) and 13.10% (30/229) after 5 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg cisPt treatment, respectively.
source: While in untreated control hybrids the late pachynemas represented 2.03% (4/107) of all pachynemas recorded from the meiotic spreads, the frequency increased to 12.12% (28/231) and 13.10% (30/229) after 5 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg cisPt treatment, respectively.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The genetic network controlling incomplete synapsis of homologous chromosomes, early meiotic arrest, and male sterility of mouse inter-subspecific PBF1 hybrids is formed by three components: Prdm9PWD/B6 heterozygosity, PWD allele at the Hstx2 locus on Chromosome X, and autosomal PWD/B6 heterozygosity.
source: The genetic network controlling incomplete synapsis of homologous chromosomes, early meiotic arrest, and male sterility of mouse inter-subspecific PBF1 hybrids is formed by three components, Prdm9PWD/B6 heterozygosity (Mihola et al., 2009), PWD allele at the Hstx2 locus on Chromosome X (Storchová et al., 2004; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014﻿ for review, see Forejt et al., 2012), and autosomal PWD/B6 heterozygosity (Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012; Gregorova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings supported by multiple citations.

claim: The molecular mechanism of the Hstx2 action is still unclear.
source: While the molecular mechanism of the Hstx2 action is still unclear, four mutually nonexclusive explanations of PRDM9-controlled meiotic arrest have been proposed.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: A divergence of fast evolving noncoding DNA and/or RNA sequences could interfere with the homology search of single-strand 3' ends on a heterosubspecific template during the DSB repair, thus interfering with chromosome synapsis.
source: Originally, we hypothesized that a divergence of fast evolving noncoding DNA and/or RNA sequences could interfere with the homology search of single-strand 3' ends on a heterosubspecific template during the DSB repair, thus interfering with chromosome synapsis (Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors in previous work.

claim: ~70% of PRDM9-directed hotspots were enriched on a 'nonself' chromosome in PBF1 hybrids.
source: Later, using our PBF1 hybrid sterility model, Davies et al. (2016) found that ~70% of PRDM9-directed hotspots were enriched on a 'nonself' chromosome (e.g. PRDM9B6 on PWD chromosome and vice versa).
evidence: This is a finding from Davies et al., 2016.

claim: DSBs in asymmetric hotspots are difficult to repair or they repair too late, perhaps using sister chromatids as a template.
source: DSBs in these hotspots are difficult to repair or they repair too late, perhaps using sister chromatids as a template (Faieta et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Chromosomal distribution of asymmetric DSB hotspots correlated well with the asynapsis rate of particular chromosomes.
source: Chromosomal distribution of asymmetric DSB hotspots correlated well with the asynapsis rate of particular chromosomes (Davies et al., 2016; Gregorova et al., 2018) and indicated that the insufficient number of DSBs generated at symmetric hotspots may limit their pairing and normal progression of spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies.

claim: The insufficient number of DSBs generated at symmetric hotspots may limit their pairing and normal progression of spermatogenesis.
source: Chromosomal distribution of asymmetric DSB hotspots correlated well with the asynapsis rate of particular chromosomes (Davies et al., 2016; Gregorova et al., 2018) and indicated that the insufficient number of DSBs generated at symmetric hotspots may limit their pairing and normal progression of spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between asymmetric hotspots and asynapsis.

claim: Addition of repairable, exogenous DSBs significantly improved the faulty synapsis of homologous chromosomes.
source: The present results show that, indeed, addition of repairable, non-DSBs in the form of exogenous DSBs significantly improved the faulty synapsis of homologous chromosomes.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current study.

claim: There is a significant enrichment of the default, PRDM9-independent DSB hotspots in PBF1 spermatocytes.
source: Another possible mechanism explaining the role of Prdm9 in meiotic arrest points to a significant enrichment of the default, PRDM9-independent DSB hotspots in PBF1 spermatocytes (Smagulova et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from Smagulova et al., 2016.

claim: Default hotspots were observed in Prdm9-/- sterile males and are preferentially located in promoters and other regulatory sequences.
source: Such hotspots were observed in Prdm9-/- sterile males and are preferentially located in promoters and other regulatory sequences.
evidence: This is established knowledge about default hotspots.

claim: About 30% of PRDM9-controlled DSBs are in repetitive sequences including transposons.
source: Finally, since a recent report uncovered about 30% of PRDM9-controlled DSBs in repetitive sequences including transposons, their homology at nonallelic sites could destabilize genome integrity and interfere with the DSB repair (Yamada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from Yamada et al., 2017.

claim: Homology of PRDM9-controlled DSBs at nonallelic sites could destabilize genome integrity and interfere with the DSB repair.
source: Finally, since a recent report uncovered about 30% of PRDM9-controlled DSBs in repetitive sequences including transposons, their homology at nonallelic sites could destabilize genome integrity and interfere with the DSB repair (Yamada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on findings from Yamada et al., 2017.

claim: The results complement previous findings bringing new evidence for the deficiency in properly repaired DSBs as one of the major causes of meiotic asynapsis and male sterility of PBF1 inter-subspecific hybrids.
source: To conclude, our results complement our previous findings (Gregorova et al., 2018) bringing new evidence for the deficiency in properly repaired DSBs as one of the major causes of meiotic asynapsis and male sterility of PBF1 inter-subspecific hybrids.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The results do not exclude the role of PRDM9 default or retroposon-directed hotspots in meiotic failure.
source: Although our results do not exclude the role of PRDM9 default or retroposon-directed hotspots in meiotic failure, they bring a new and independent evidence in favor of DSB hotspot asymmetry caused by PRDM9 hotspot erasure as the main cause of chromosome asynapsis and meiotic arrest in PBF1 intersubspecific hybrid sterility.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations and implications of the findings.

claim: The results bring new and independent evidence in favor of DSB hotspot asymmetry caused by PRDM9 hotspot erasure as the main cause of chromosome asynapsis and meiotic arrest in PBF1 intersubspecific hybrid sterility.
source: Although our results do not exclude the role of PRDM9 default or retroposon-directed hotspots in meiotic failure, they bring a new and independent evidence in favor of DSB hotspot asymmetry caused by PRDM9 hotspot erasure as the main cause of chromosome asynapsis and meiotic arrest in PBF1 intersubspecific hybrid sterility.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
